instrument_or_setup.value: Fischerscope H100 microhardness tester (maximum load 1 N)

key_findings.value: Heat treatment changes HU by only about 5–10% around 2000 N/mm²; the 1100 °C Q + 300 °C/14 d condition shows the highest hardness (>2050 N/mm²). Short-range ordering has no major impact on hardness.

measurement_conditions.value: room temperature; HU = F/(26.43·h²) [N/mm²] with indentation force F and depth h; reported HU values are averages of more than 40 measurements

purpose.value: Determine the effect of prior heat treatment (including 1100 °C Q + 300 °C/14 d) on the hardness of (111)-oriented Fe-16%Al monocrystals

source.reason: b0018 describes the Fischerscope H100 microhardness method and the HU formula; Fig. 1 / b0050 report the hardness vs heat-treatment results.

key_findings.value: The '1100°C Q + 300°C/14d' condition gives the highest plateau stress (~450–500 MPa); the effect of heat treatment on the flow stress is only modest.

measurement_conditions.value: room temperature, compression rate 10^-4 s^-1; specimen dimensions 5×5×10 mm; monocrystals polished with 3 µm diamond paste; 0.2% proof stress

purpose.value: Study the compressive stress-strain behaviour of the [112]-oriented Fe-16%Al monocrystal as a function of prior heat treatment

source.reason: b0019 describes the compression-test procedure (0.2% proof stress, rates, specimen dimensions); Fig. 2 / b0031 report the compressive stress-strain results.

interaction_type.value: excess vacancies acting as obstacles to dislocation movement

qualitative_or_quantitative_description.value: Excess vacancies produced by the 1100 °C quench are immobile at low temperature, are effective obstacles to dislocation movement and contribute to hardening; they are only slowly healed out by the 300 °C/14 d anneal.

interface_notes.value: The sample is a monocrystal with no grain boundaries; the only second phase are rare globular AlN inclusions (up to 30 µm). Interfaces were not further characterized in this work.

source.reason: b0026 reports the AlN inclusions in the Fe-16%Al monocrystal; b0055 describes the hardening role of quenched-in excess vacancies (immobile obstacles to dislocations) and their slow healing-out during the 300 °C anneal.

method.value: high-temperature treatment (solution treatment) followed by water quench

processing_steps_notes.value: This is the 'Q*' condition (water quench from 1100 °C) applied to the (111)/[112] Fe-16%Al monocrystal. Per b0015, heat treatments at 1100 °C were usually only 15 min and (except for short treatments up to 300 °C) specimens were enclosed in evacuated (10^-6 bar) SiO2 capsules. Quenching from 1100 °C suppresses short-range order nearly completely and traps excess vacancies.

source.reason: Process definition (water quench from 1100 °C) plus the experimental details on 1100 °C heat-treatment duration/capsule (b0015) and the Q* definition in the Fig. 1 caption (b0033).

processing_steps_notes.value: Anneal after the 1100 °C water quench, intended to heal out excess vacancies. Reported to only slightly reduce the quenched hardness; 14 days at 300 °C may not be sufficient for complete elimination of the excess vacancies. (b0015 states that heat treatments at temperatures up to 300 °C were performed in argon of 99.99% purity.)

overall_structure.value: Single-crystal (Bridgman-grown) Fe-16%Al monocrystal; no grain boundaries; contains rare globular AlN inclusions; after 1100 °C quench + 300 °C/14 d anneal it retains quenched-in excess vacancies (only partially healed out).

source.reason: The Fe-16%Al monocrystals were grown by the Bridgman method (b0014); b0026 reports the monocrystals contain rare globular AlN inclusions up to 30 µm identified by EDX; b0055 describes the quenched-in excess vacancies whose healing-out is slow in these quenched Fe-Al alloys.

unmapped_findings: Sample composition (Table 1, monocrystal nominal 16 at.% Al): real Al content 16.0 at.% (8.4 wt.-%), impurities C 45 wt.ppm, Si 40 wt.ppm, O 60 wt.ppm.

Quenching from 1100 °C produces excess vacancies that contribute to hardening; the 300 °C anneal after quenching reduces the quenched hardness only slightly, and even 14 days at 300 °C may not be sufficient for complete elimination of the excess vacancies (slow healing-out kinetics).

The present results contrast with Davies, who reported a 25% increase of the yield stress of a quenched Fe-16.5%Al alloy by a short 1 h anneal at 300 °C (alloy preparation and impurity content not given).

Related but distinct treatment (NOT this sample's 300 °C anneal): no carbides were detected in the Fe-16%Al monocrystal with 45 ppm C after a heat treatment of 14 days at 320 °C; without any heat treatment no carbides were found in any monocrystal (b0026).
